topic.subject: social
topic.title: Money and credit
topic.scope: barter and double coincidence of wants, money as medium of exchange, banks and deposits, credit, collateral, SHGs

misconceptions.statement: Barter is efficient if you have enough goods to trade.
misconceptions.why: Students assume that having more goods automatically solves the problem of finding a buyer.
misconceptions.fix: Barter requires both parties to want exactly what the other has, which is rare and difficult to coordinate.

probe.question: Why is barter difficult even if you have many goods?
probe.wrong_answer: Because you just need to find someone who wants your goods.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Modern paper money has intrinsic value like gold or silver.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the physical material of money with its legal status as a medium of exchange.
misconceptions.fix: Modern money has no intrinsic value; it is accepted because the government authorizes it as a medium of exchange.

probe.question: Why is a 500 rupee note valuable?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the paper is special or it represents gold in the bank.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Collateral is a fee paid to the bank for taking a loan.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse collateral with interest or processing charges.
misconceptions.fix: Collateral is an asset owned by the borrower that serves as a guarantee to the lender until the loan is repaid.

probe.question: What happens to collateral after the loan is repaid?
probe.wrong_answer: The bank keeps it as a service fee.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: The RBI directly gives loans to small farmers and businesses.
misconceptions.why: Students conflate the regulatory role of the central bank with the retail role of commercial banks.
misconceptions.fix: The RBI supervises banks to ensure they follow rules, but it does not lend money to the public.

probe.question: Who should a farmer approach for a loan?

misconceptions.statement: Money is valuable only because it can be saved, not because people accept it in exchange.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the visible act of keeping money and overlook its role as a medium of exchange.
misconceptions.fix: Money is valuable because everyone accepts it in payment for goods and services; this removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.

probe.question: Why do shopkeepers accept currency notes in return for goods?
probe.wrong_answer: Because notes can be saved in a purse or bank for a long time.

misconceptions.root_belief: Money's worth comes from storage, not acceptance

misconceptions.statement: Any currency note or coin can be legally refused by a seller, since only the government accepts it.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse everyday willingness to accept money with its legal status.
misconceptions.fix: In India the Reserve Bank of India issues currency notes, and the law makes them legal tender, so no one can refuse payment in rupees for settling a transaction.

probe.question: Can a person legally refuse to accept rupees as payment for a debt in India?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, only the government is bound to accept rupee notes.

misconceptions.root_belief: Legal tender is just custom, not law

misconceptions.statement: Cheques are money in the same way that currency notes are.
misconceptions.why: Students see cheques being used to pay for things and treat them as currency itself.
misconceptions.fix: A cheque is only an instruction to the bank to pay from a deposit; the money is the balance in the account, and a cheque payment is not legal tender.

probe.question: When you pay by cheque, what is actually being transferred?
probe.wrong_answer: The cheque itself is the money being handed over.

misconceptions.root_belief: Anything used for payment is itself money
misconceptions.source_hint: economics education research on money concepts

misconceptions.statement: The bank keeps all deposited money in its vault until depositors withdraw it.
misconceptions.why: Students imagine a bank as a safe, not as a lender.
misconceptions.fix: Banks keep only a small part of deposits as cash for daily withdrawals and lend out most of it, earning more interest on loans than they pay on deposits.

probe.question: What do banks do with the money people deposit?
probe.wrong_answer: They store all of it safely until people take it back.

misconceptions.root_belief: Banks only store money, never lend it
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student understanding of banking

misconceptions.statement: Interest on a deposit and interest on a loan are the same rate, so the bank earns nothing.
misconceptions.why: Students think of interest as one fixed number rather than two different rates.
misconceptions.fix: Banks charge a higher interest rate on loans than they pay on deposits, and the difference is their main source of income.

probe.question: How do banks make a profit from deposits and loans?
probe.wrong_answer: They cannot make a profit as both rates are equal; they only charge service fees.

misconceptions.root_belief: Interest rates are single and uniform

misconceptions.statement: The terms of credit are fixed by law, so every borrower gets the same interest rate and conditions.
misconceptions.why: Students assume formal rules make credit uniform for everyone.
misconceptions.fix: Terms of credit such as interest rate, collateral, documentation and repayment mode vary between lenders and borrowers; they are agreed, not identical for all.

probe.question: Two farmers borrow from different lenders. Will their interest rate and repayment terms be the same?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, the law fixes one interest rate and repayment rule for everyone.

misconceptions.root_belief: Credit terms are uniform and fixed

misconceptions.statement: Collateral is taken only from poor borrowers, and the lender keeps it even after the loan is repaid.
misconceptions.why: Students link collateral with suspicion of the borrower and with a penalty.
misconceptions.fix: Collateral, such as land or a house, is security the lender holds against non-payment; it is returned when the loan is fully repaid and sold only if the borrower defaults.

probe.question: A farmer repays his loan fully. What happens to the land papers he gave as collateral?
probe.wrong_answer: The bank keeps them because collateral belongs to the bank.

misconceptions.root_belief: Collateral is ownership transferred to the lender

misconceptions.statement: Self Help Groups give loans only from outside funds, with no savings needed from members.
misconceptions.why: Students think of SHGs as charity or a government scheme, not a savings group.
misconceptions.fix: SHG members, usually women, pool small regular savings, and the group gives loans from this pool at reasonable interest, often later linked to banks.

probe.question: Where does the money for loans in a Self Help Group first come from?
probe.wrong_answer: From government grants, not from members' savings.

misconceptions.root_belief: SHG is a charity, not member savings
